note.explanation: Measurements use numbers and units. This chapter explains how to choose units and instruments, record readings carefully, use prefixes and scientific notation, and handle errors and significant digits.
examples: A desk height may be measured in metres (m).
A thickness may be measured with a micrometer screw gauge.
note.checkAnswer: A standard unit lets different people compare measurements consistently.
note.simple: A measurement tells how much of something there is. It needs a number and a unit.
note.checkQuestion: Why do we need a standard unit for measurements?
note.title: Measuring physical quantities
steps: Choose an appropriate instrument and unit.
Read the instrument carefully, avoiding viewing errors.
Record the number with its unit.
Use prefixes or scientific notation when useful.
note.answer: A measurement consists of a numerical value and a unit.

mcqs.stem: Q1.1. The instrument that is most suitable for measuring the thickness of a few sheets of cardboard is:
rationales: A metre rule is not precise enough for a few sheets.
A measuring tape is intended for larger lengths.
Vernier Callipers can measure small thicknesses but are less suitable than a micrometer for this very small thickness.
A micrometer screw gauge is the most suitable choice for measuring a small thickness precisely.

mcqs.stem: Q1.2. One femtometre is equal to:
rationales: 10⁻⁹ m is a nanometre, not a femtometre.
The prefix femto means 10⁻¹⁵.
10⁹ m is not the femto scale.
10¹⁵ m is not the femto scale.

mcqs.stem: Q1.3. A light year is a unit of:
rationales: A light year is not a measure of light itself.
A year is a time interval, but a light year is not a time unit.
A light year is the distance light travels in one year.
Speed is distance per unit time, not a light year.

mcqs.stem: Q1.4. Which one is a non-physical quantity?
rationales: Distance is measurable, so it is physical.
Density is measurable, so it is physical.
Colour, as stated here, is not a physical quantity measured as a numerical quantity with a unit.
Temperature is measurable, so it is physical.

options: look at the meniscus from below the level of the water surface
take several readings by looking from more than one direction
position the eye in line with the bottom of the meniscus
mcqs.stem: Q1.5. When using a measuring cylinder, one precaution to take is to:
rationales: Zero error is not the precaution being tested for a measuring cylinder reading here.
Looking from below the surface causes a viewing error.
Looking from different directions does not give a correct meniscus reading.
The eye should be in line with the bottom of the meniscus to avoid parallax error.

mcqs.stem: Q1.6. Volume of water consumed by you per day is estimated in:
rationales: A millilitre is too small a convenient unit for a daily amount.
A litre is an appropriate unit for daily water consumption.
A kilogram is a unit of mass, not volume.
A cubic metre is much too large for this estimate.

mcqs.stem: Q1.7. A displacement can is used to measure:
rationales: A displacement can does not measure mass.
A displacement can does not measure mass.
It is used to find the volume of an irregular solid by displacement, not the volume of a liquid.
The displaced liquid gives the volume of a solid.

mcqs.stem: Q1.8. Two rods with lengths 12.321 cm and 10.3 cm are placed side by side, the difference in their lengths is:
rationales: The subtraction is 2.021 cm, but the result should be rounded to the least precise decimal place, tenths.
12.321 − 10.3 = 2.021 cm, rounded to one decimal place gives 2.0 cm.
2 cm loses the tenths place required by the measurement rule.
2.021 cm reports unjustified precision.

mcqs.stem: Q1.9. Four students measure the diameter of a cylinder with Vernier Callipers. Which of the following readings is correct?
rationales: This does not report the reading to the appropriate precision.
This gives too many decimal places for the usual Vernier Callipers reading shown by the choices.
3.47 cm is the reading expressed to the appropriate precision.
3.5 cm is too coarsely recorded.

mcqs.stem: Q1.10. Which of the following measures are likely to represent the thickness of a sheet of this book?
rationales: This is far too small for a book sheet.
10⁻⁴ m is a plausible sheet thickness.
This is a nuclear-scale length and far too small.
This is 4 cm, far too thick for a sheet.

mcqs.stem: Q1.11. In a Vernier Callipers ten smallest divisions of the Vernier scale are equal to nine smallest divisions of the main scale. If the smallest division of the main scale is half millimetre, the Vernier constant is equal to:
rationales: 0.5 mm is one main-scale division, not the Vernier constant.
One Vernier division is 0.45 mm, so the difference is 0.05 mm, not 0.1 mm.
One main-scale division is 0.5 mm; one Vernier division is 9 × 0.5 ÷ 10 = 0.45 mm, so the difference is 0.05 mm.
0.001 mm is too small and does not follow from the given scales.

written.text: Can a non-physical quantity be measured? If yes, then how?
written.finalAnswer: Yes. It can be measured by defining a suitable scale or method and assigning values.

rubric.why: A non-physical quantity has no direct physical measuring unit.
rubric.description: Explain how it can be quantified.
rubric.how: Describe a defined scale or method.

rubric.why: The answer must directly address whether it can be measured.
rubric.how: Answer yes, with the qualification above.

modelAnswer: Yes, a non-physical quantity can be measured by defining a suitable scale or method and assigning values to it.

written.text: What is measurement? Name its two parts.
written.finalAnswer: A measurement consists of a numerical value and a unit.

rubric.why: A measurement must state the amount.
rubric.how: State that it has a number or numerical value.

rubric.why: The unit identifies the standard used for the amount.
rubric.how: State that a measurement includes a unit.

modelAnswer: Measurement is the comparison of an unknown quantity with a standard quantity of the same kind.
Its two parts are a numerical value and a unit.

written.text: Why do we need a standard unit for measurements?
written.finalAnswer: A standard unit makes measurements consistent and comparable.

rubric.why: Standards avoid different results caused by personal units.
rubric.how: Say that a standard gives uniform measurements.

rubric.why: Common units let people compare measurements.
rubric.how: State that measurements made by different people can be compared.

modelAnswer: A standard unit is needed so that measurements are uniform and can be compared everywhere.

written.text: Write the name of 3 base quantities and 3 derived quantities.
written.finalAnswer: Base: length, mass, time. Derived: area, volume, density.

rubric.why: These are examples of base quantities.
These are quantities derived from base quantities.

modelAnswer: Base quantities: length, mass and time.
Derived quantities: area, volume and density.

written.text: Which SI unit will you use to express the height of your desk?

rubric.why: The height is a length and its SI unit is the metre.

modelAnswer: The height of a desk is expressed in metre (m).

written.text: Write the name and symbols of all SI base units.
written.finalAnswer: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd).

rubric.why: The first four SI base units must be identified correctly.
rubric.how: List metre, kilogram, second and ampere with symbols.

rubric.why: The remaining SI base units complete the list.
rubric.how: List kelvin, mole and candela with symbols.

modelAnswer: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd).

written.text: Why prefix is used? Name three sub-multiple and three multiple prefixes with their symbols.
written.finalAnswer: Prefixes express very large or very small quantities conveniently; examples include milli (m), micro (μ), nano (n), kilo (k), mega (M), giga (G).

rubric.why: Prefixes simplify expressing quantities at different scales.
rubric.how: Say they represent large or small multiples conveniently.

rubric.why: Examples must include both sub-multiples and multiples.
rubric.how: Give three sub-multiples and three multiples with symbols.

modelAnswer: A prefix is used to express very large or very small quantities conveniently.
Sub-multiples: milli (m), micro (μ), nano (n).
Multiples: kilo (k), mega (M), giga (G).

written.text: What is meant by: (a) 5 pm (b) 15 ns (c) 6 μm (d) 5 fs

rubric.why: These identify the first two prefix-unit quantities.
rubric.how: Expand pico and nano with the unit.

rubric.why: These identify the remaining prefix-unit quantities.
rubric.how: Expand micro and femto with the unit.

modelAnswer: (a) 5 pm = 5 picometres.
(b) 15 ns = 15 nanoseconds.
(c) 6 μm = 6 micrometres.
(d) 5 fs = 5 femtoseconds.

written.text: (a) For what purpose, a Vernier Callipers is used? (b) Name its two main parts. (c) How is least count found? (d) What is meant by zero error?
written.finalAnswer: It measures small lengths, internal/external diameters and depths; its main scale and Vernier scale; least count is one main-scale division minus one Vernier-scale division; zero error is a non-zero reading when the jaws are closed.

rubric.why: The instrument's use must be identified.
Both scales are essential parts.
rubric.how: Give the main scale and Vernier scale.

rubric.why: The least count is determined from the difference between scale divisions.
rubric.how: State the difference between one main-scale division and one Vernier-scale division.

rubric.why: Zero error is a reading that remains when the instrument should read zero.
rubric.how: Describe a non-zero reading with the jaws closed.

modelAnswer: (a) Vernier Callipers are used to measure small lengths, internal and external diameters, and depths.
(b) Its two main parts are the main scale and the Vernier scale.
(c) Least count = one main-scale division − one Vernier-scale division.
(d) Zero error is the reading shown when the jaws are closed instead of zero.

written.text: State least count and Vernier scale reading as shown in the figure and hence, find the length.
written.finalAnswer: Cannot be determined from the supplied figure description: it shows ruler readings, not Vernier scale divisions.

rubric.why: The supplied figure description gives only ruler/viewing readings.
rubric.how: State that the listed figure readings are 5.9 cm, 6.0 cm and 6.1 cm.

rubric.why: A Vernier reading and least count need scale divisions that are absent from the described figure.
rubric.how: Point out the figure description does not provide Vernier divisions.

modelAnswer: The supplied figure description shows ruler readings 5.9 cm, 6.0 cm and 6.1 cm, not a Vernier scale.
Therefore the least count, Vernier scale reading and requested length cannot be determined from the supplied figure description.

written.text: Which reading out of A, B and C shows the correct length and why?
written.finalAnswer: B, 6.0 cm, because the eye is in line with the object and scale reading.

rubric.why: The middle viewing position avoids parallax error.
The reason is the eye's correct alignment with the reading.
rubric.how: State that the eye is level with the reading, avoiding parallax.

modelAnswer: B, 6.0 cm, is correct.
The eye is in line with the object and the scale reading, so parallax error is avoided.

written.text: In what unit will you express each of the following? (a) Thickness of a five-rupee coin: _____

rubric.why: A coin's small thickness is conveniently expressed in millimetres.

modelAnswer: (a) Thickness of a five-rupee coin: millimetre (mm).

written.text: In what unit will you express each of the following? (b) Length of a book: _____

rubric.why: A book's length is conveniently expressed in centimetres.

modelAnswer: (b) Length of a book: centimetre (cm).

written.text: In what unit will you express each of the following? (c) Length of football field: _____

rubric.why: A football field length is conveniently expressed in metres.

modelAnswer: (c) Length of football field: metre (m).

written.text: In what unit will you express each of the following? (d) The distance between two cities: _____

rubric.why: City-to-city distances are conveniently expressed in kilometres.

modelAnswer: (d) The distance between two cities: kilometre (km).

written.text: In what unit will you express each of the following? (e) Mass of five-rupee coin: _____

rubric.why: A coin's mass is conveniently expressed in grams.

modelAnswer: (e) Mass of a five-rupee coin: gram (g).

written.text: In what unit will you express each of the following? (f) Mass of your school bag: _____

rubric.why: A school bag's mass is conveniently expressed in kilograms.

modelAnswer: (f) Mass of your school bag: kilogram (kg).

written.text: In what unit will you express each of the following? (g) Duration of your class period: _____

rubric.why: A class period is conveniently expressed in minutes.

modelAnswer: (g) Duration of your class period: minute (min).

written.text: In what unit will you express each of the following? (h) Volume of petrol filled in the tank of a car: _____

rubric.why: Petrol volumes are commonly expressed in litres.

modelAnswer: (h) Volume of petrol filled in the tank of a car: litre (L).

written.text: In what unit will you express each of the following? (i) Time to boil one litre milk: _____

rubric.why: This everyday time interval is conveniently expressed in minutes.

modelAnswer: (i) Time to boil one litre milk: minute (min).

written.text: Why might a standard system of measurement be helpful to a tailor?
written.finalAnswer: It lets the tailor take and communicate consistent body and cloth measurements so clothes fit correctly.

rubric.why: Standard units make measurements consistent.
rubric.how: State that it avoids differing measurement conventions.

rubric.why: The measurements are used to make properly fitting clothes.
rubric.how: Mention accurate garment sizing or fit.

modelAnswer: A standard system gives the tailor consistent body and cloth measurements.
This helps the tailor make clothes of the correct size and fit.

written.text: The minimum main scale reading of a micrometer screw gauge is 1 mm and there are 100 divisions on the circular scale. When thimble is rotated once, 1 mm is its measurement on the main scale. What is the least count of the instrument? The reading for thickness of a steel rod as shown in the figure. What is the thickness of the rod?
written.finalAnswer: Least count = 0.01 mm; thickness = 0.70 mm (assuming the figure's circular-scale reading is 70 and main-scale reading is 0 mm).

rubric.why: The least count is pitch divided by the number of circular divisions.
The scale reading is obtained by multiplying circular divisions by least count and combining with main-scale reading.
rubric.how: Use the stated assumption that the circular scale shows 70 and main scale shows 0 mm.

rubric.why: A measured thickness must have a unit.
rubric.description: Give the result with its unit.

modelAnswer: Pitch = 1 mm; number of circular-scale divisions = 100.
Least count = pitch ÷ number of divisions = 1 mm ÷ 100 = 0.01 mm.
Assuming the shown circular-scale reading is 70 and the main-scale reading is 0 mm: thickness = 0 mm + (70 × 0.01 mm).
Thickness of the rod = 0.70 mm.

written.text: You are provided a metre scale and a bundle of pencils; how can the diameter of a pencil be measured using the metre scale with the same precision as that of Vernier Callipers? Describe briefly.
written.finalAnswer: Arrange several pencils tightly side by side, measure their total width with the metre scale, then divide by the number of pencils.

rubric.why: Measuring several equal diameters together reduces the relative effect of scale precision.
rubric.how: Arrange a known number of pencils tightly side by side.

rubric.why: The overall width must be measured with the available scale.
Dividing the total by the number gives one pencil's diameter.
rubric.how: Divide the total width by the number of pencils.

modelAnswer: Place a known number of pencils tightly side by side in a straight row.
Measure the total width of the row with the metre scale.
Divide the total width by the number of pencils.
The quotient is the diameter of one pencil, measured more precisely by using the combined width.

written.text: The end of a metre scale is worn out. Where will you place a pencil to find the length?
written.finalAnswer: Place one end of the pencil at a clear mark, such as the 1 cm mark, and subtract the starting reading from the ending reading.

rubric.why: A worn zero end cannot be relied on.
rubric.how: Place the pencil at a clear scale mark away from the worn end.

rubric.why: The length is the difference between final and initial readings.
rubric.how: Subtract the starting reading from the ending reading.

modelAnswer: Place one end of the pencil at a clear mark on the metre scale, for example the 1 cm mark.
Read the other end and subtract the starting reading from it to find the length.

written.text: Why is it better to place the object close to the metre scale?
written.finalAnswer: It reduces parallax error when reading the scale.

rubric.why: The object should be aligned with the scale marks.
rubric.how: Say that the object is placed close to the scale.

rubric.why: This limits reading error caused by separation from the scale.
rubric.how: State that it reduces parallax error and improves accuracy.

modelAnswer: The object should be close to the metre scale so it lines up with the scale marks.
This reduces parallax error and gives a more accurate reading.

written.text: Why a standard unit is needed to measure a quantity correctly?
written.finalAnswer: A standard unit gives a uniform, agreed value that can be compared and communicated reliably.

rubric.why: A common unit prevents inconsistent measurements.
rubric.how: State that the unit is agreed and uniform.

rubric.why: Standard units allow reliable comparison and communication.
rubric.how: Mention comparison or communication of results.

modelAnswer: A standard unit is needed to make measurements uniform and correct.
It allows people to compare and communicate measurements reliably.

written.text: Suggest some natural phenomena that could serve as a reasonably accurate time standard.
written.finalAnswer: Regular astronomical phenomena, such as Earth's rotation, Earth's revolution around the Sun, and the Moon's revolution around Earth.

rubric.why: A regular cycle can be used to mark time.
rubric.description: Give an example of a natural cycle.

rubric.why: Another regular natural cycle is an acceptable time standard.
rubric.how: Name the Moon's revolution or another regular astronomical cycle.

modelAnswer: Earth's rotation about its axis can serve as a time standard.
Earth's revolution around the Sun and the Moon's revolution around Earth are other natural periodic phenomena.

written.text: It is difficult to locate the meniscus in a wider vessel. Why?
written.finalAnswer: In a wide vessel the curved surface is less clearly defined, so its exact lowest point is harder to locate.

rubric.why: The difficulty relates to identifying the liquid surface in a wide vessel.
rubric.how: Refer to the meniscus or curved surface.

rubric.why: A less distinct curve makes the correct reading point uncertain.
rubric.how: State that its exact level or lowest point is hard to see.

modelAnswer: In a wider vessel the curved meniscus is less clearly defined.
Therefore it is difficult to locate its exact lowest point accurately.

written.text: Which instrument can be used to measure: (i) internal diameter of a test tube (ii) depth of a beaker?
written.finalAnswer: (i) Vernier Callipers (ii) Vernier Callipers, using its depth gauge.

rubric.why: The internal jaws measure internal diameter.
Its depth gauge measures depth.
rubric.how: Give Vernier Callipers with its depth gauge.

modelAnswer: (i) Internal diameter of a test tube: Vernier Callipers, using its inside jaws.
(ii) Depth of a beaker: Vernier Callipers, using its depth gauge.

written.text: What is meant by base and derived quantities? Give the names and symbols of SI base units.
written.finalAnswer: Base quantities are independent quantities; derived quantities are obtained from them. SI base units: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd).

rubric.why: Base quantities are defined independently.
rubric.how: State that they are independent quantities.

rubric.why: Derived quantities are formed from base quantities.
rubric.how: State that they are obtained from base quantities.

rubric.why: The SI base-unit list must include the first four units.
rubric.how: Name and symbolize metre, kilogram, second and ampere.

rubric.why: The remaining three units complete the SI base-unit list.
rubric.how: Name and symbolize kelvin, mole and candela.

modelAnswer: Base quantities are independent quantities that are not defined in terms of other physical quantities.
Derived quantities are obtained from base quantities.
The SI base units are metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol) and candela (cd).

written.text: Give three examples of derived unit in SI. How are they derived from base units? Describe briefly.
written.finalAnswer: Examples: area (m²), speed (m s⁻¹), and density (kg m⁻³), derived by combining base units according to their definitions.

rubric.why: Area is a derived quantity with unit square metre.
Speed is distance divided by time.
Density is mass divided by volume.
Derived units follow from the defining equation of each quantity.
rubric.how: Describe multiplication or division of base units.

modelAnswer: Area = length × length, so its SI unit is m × m = m².
Speed = distance ÷ time, so its SI unit is m s⁻¹.
Density = mass ÷ volume, so its SI unit is kg m⁻³.
Derived units are formed by combining base units according to the definitions of the quantities.

written.text: State the similarities and differences between Vernier Callipers and micrometer screw gauge.
written.finalAnswer: Both measure small lengths accurately. Vernier Callipers use main and Vernier scales and are useful for diameters and depths; a micrometer uses a screw and circular scale and is especially suited to small thicknesses or diameters.

rubric.why: Both instruments measure small dimensions accurately.
rubric.how: Mention accurate measurement of small lengths.

rubric.why: These identify the Vernier Callipers scales.
rubric.how: Name its main and Vernier scales.

rubric.why: These identify the micrometer's measuring mechanism.
rubric.how: Mention its screw and circular scale or thimble.

rubric.why: The instruments have different useful applications.
rubric.how: Give suitable measurements for each instrument.

modelAnswer: Both Vernier Callipers and a micrometer screw gauge measure small lengths accurately.
Vernier Callipers have a main scale and a Vernier scale; they can measure external and internal diameters and depths.
A micrometer screw gauge uses a screw, sleeve scale and circular scale; it is especially suitable for small thicknesses and diameters.

written.text: Identify and explain the reasons for human errors, random errors and systematic errors in experiments.
written.finalAnswer: Human errors arise from mistakes by the observer; random errors vary unpredictably between readings; systematic errors shift readings consistently because of an instrument or method fault.

rubric.why: Human errors originate in the observer's actions or judgement.
rubric.how: Give an observer mistake, such as misreading or recording.

rubric.why: Random errors change irregularly across measurements.
Systematic errors produce a consistent bias.
rubric.how: Name an instrument or method cause.

rubric.why: An example clarifies the error source.
rubric.description: Give a suitable cause or example.
rubric.how: Mention zero error, poor calibration, or a consistent method fault.

modelAnswer: Human errors are caused by the observer, for example misreading or incorrectly recording a scale.
Random errors cause readings to vary unpredictably from one measurement to another.
Systematic errors cause readings to be consistently too high or too low, often because of zero error, poor calibration or a faulty method.

written.text: Differentiate between precision and accuracy of a measurement with examples.
written.finalAnswer: Precision is how close repeated measurements are to one another; accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value.

rubric.why: Precision concerns agreement among repeated measurements.
rubric.how: State that repeated readings are close to one another.

rubric.why: Accuracy concerns closeness to the true value.
rubric.how: State that a reading is close to the true value.

rubric.why: An example shows the difference in practice.
rubric.how: Provide readings that are precise or accurate.

rubric.why: Precision and accuracy are not identical concepts.
rubric.how: Note that repeated readings can agree without being near the true value.

modelAnswer: Precision describes how close repeated measurements are to one another.
Accuracy describes how close a measurement is to the true value.
For example, repeated readings of 5.1 cm, 5.1 cm and 5.2 cm are precise; if the true value is 5.1 cm, they are also accurate.
A set of readings can be precise but inaccurate if they agree with one another but differ from the true value.

written.text: Calculate the number of seconds in a (a) day and state your answer using SI prefixes.

rubric.why: The day must be converted to seconds correctly.
The answer must use the requested SI prefix.

written.text: Calculate the number of seconds in a (b) week and state your answer using SI prefixes.

rubric.why: The week must be converted to seconds correctly.
The answer must use the requested SI prefix.

written.text: Calculate the number of seconds in a (c) month and state your answer using SI prefixes.

rubric.why: The month is taken as 30 days in the stated result.
The answer must use the requested SI prefix.

written.text: State the answer of problem 1.1(a) in scientific notation.

rubric.why: The correct number of seconds in a day is needed.
Scientific notation must be normalized and include the unit.

written.text: State the answer of problem 1.1(b) in scientific notation.

rubric.why: The correct number of seconds in a week is needed.
Scientific notation must be normalized and include the unit.

written.text: State the answer of problem 1.1(c) in scientific notation.

rubric.why: The month is taken as 30 days for this problem.
Scientific notation must be normalized and include the unit.

written.text: Solve the following addition or subtraction. State your answers in scientific notation. (a) 4 × 10⁻⁴ kg + 3 × 10⁻⁵ kg

rubric.why: Terms must be expressed with matching powers before adding.
The final sum and unit must be correct.

written.text: Solve the following addition or subtraction. State your answers in scientific notation. (b) 5.4 × 10⁻⁶ m − 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ m

rubric.why: The powers of ten must be made equal before subtracting.
The negative sign, value and unit are essential.

written.text: Solve the following multiplication or division. State your answers in scientific notation. (a) (5 × 10⁴ m) × (3 × 10⁻² m)

rubric.why: Coefficients, powers and units must be multiplied correctly.
The normalized result and squared length unit are required.

written.text: Solve the following multiplication or division. State your answers in scientific notation. (b) (6 × 10⁸ kg)/(3 × 10⁴ m³)

rubric.why: Divide coefficients and subtract exponents correctly.
The final scientific notation and compound unit must be correct.

written.text: Calculate the following and state your answer in scientific notation. ((3 × 10² kg) × (4.0 km))/(5 × 10² s²)

rubric.why: The distance must be converted from kilometres to metres.
Numerator and denominator must be substituted and evaluated correctly.
rubric.how: Show the coefficient and power calculations.

rubric.why: The result must be normalized with the correct dimensions.
The final answer and unit must match the stated result.

modelAnswer: = 2.4 × 10³ kg m s⁻².

written.text: State the number of significant digits in each measurement. (a) 0.0045 m

rubric.why: Leading zeros do not count as significant digits.
The requested answer is the count.

modelAnswer: In 0.0045 m, the leading zeros are not significant.
There are 2 significant digits.

written.text: State the number of significant digits in each measurement. (b) 2.047 m

rubric.why: The zero between non-zero digits is significant.
The requested answer is the count.

modelAnswer: In 2.047 m, the zero between non-zero digits is significant.
There are 4 significant digits.

written.text: State the number of significant digits in each measurement. (c) 3.40 m

rubric.why: The trailing zero after a decimal point is significant.
The requested answer is the count.

modelAnswer: In 3.40 m, the zero after the decimal point is significant.
There are 3 significant digits.

written.text: State the number of significant digits in each measurement. (d) 3.420 × 10⁴ m

rubric.why: Significant digits are counted in the coefficient.
The requested answer is the count.

modelAnswer: In 3.420 × 10⁴ m, the coefficient has four significant digits.
There are 4 significant digits.

written.text: Write in scientific notation: (a) 0.0035 m

rubric.why: The decimal must be moved to give a coefficient from 1 to 10.
The exponent and unit must be correct.

written.text: Write in scientific notation: (b) 206.4 × 10² m

rubric.why: The coefficient must be normalized while accounting for the decimal shift.
The total exponent and unit must be correct.
rubric.how: Combine 10² from the decimal shift with the original 10².

written.text: Write using correct prefixes: (a) 5.0 × 10⁴ cm

rubric.why: The centimetres must be converted to metres correctly.
The final quantity must use the appropriate prefix.

written.text: Write using correct prefixes: (b) 580 × 10² g

rubric.why: The value must first be evaluated in grams.
The grams must be expressed with the correct prefix.

written.text: Write using correct prefixes: (c) 45 × 10⁻⁴ s

rubric.why: The value must be expressed as a power of ten in seconds.
The final value must use the milli prefix.

written.text: Light year is a unit of distance used in Astronomy. It is the distance covered by light in one year. Taking the speed of light as 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, calculate the distance.

rubric.why: The given speed must be identified for use in the distance relation.
Distance is calculated from speed multiplied by time, with one year expressed in seconds.
rubric.how: Use d = vt and t = 365 × 24 × 60 × 60 s.

rubric.why: Substitution and multiplication must be shown.
rubric.how: Multiply the speed by the seconds in a year.

rubric.why: The final value, rounding and metre unit must be correct.

modelAnswer: Given: speed of light, v = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; time, t = 1 year.
Formula: distance = speed × time, d = vt.

explain.title: Physical quantities and units
explain.body: A physical quantity can be measured and expressed using a number and a unit. Base quantities are independent; derived quantities are formed from base quantities. The SI base units are metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol) and candela (cd).

explain.title: Choosing instruments and reading them
explain.body: Choose an instrument suited to the size being measured. Vernier Callipers use a main scale and Vernier scale; a micrometer screw gauge is useful for very small thicknesses. Read scales with the eye level with the mark or meniscus to avoid parallax error.

explain.title: Prefixes and scientific notation
explain.body: Prefixes such as kilo, milli, micro and nano make very large or small quantities easier to write. Scientific notation writes a number as a coefficient from 1 to 10 multiplied by a power of 10.

explain.title: Significant digits and calculations
explain.body: Significant digits communicate the precision of a measurement. Leading zeros are not significant; zeros between non-zero digits and trailing decimal zeros are significant. In addition and subtraction, align powers of ten; in multiplication and division, combine powers.

explain.title: Errors, precision and accuracy
explain.body: Human errors come from the observer. Random errors vary unpredictably, while systematic errors create a consistent shift. Precision is agreement between repeated measurements; accuracy is closeness to the true value.

mistakes: Choosing an instrument that is too coarse for the size being measured.
Looking at a scale or meniscus from above or below, causing parallax error.
Writing a measurement without its unit or using a unit for the wrong quantity.
Adding or subtracting numbers in scientific notation before making their powers of ten the same.
Counting leading zeros as significant digits or ignoring a trailing decimal zero.
Forgetting to convert units before substituting into a formula, especially kilometres to metres or centimetres cubed to metres cubed.
Reporting an answer with unjustified precision or omitting the requested SI prefix.
